title: An Algorithm-Free Feed for $1,999/month
content:
Like many creatives, Adam Ayers, the former CTO of Yeezy, and his wife, Victoria de la Fuente, who worked in the fashion industry, were sick of algorithms warping their experience of social media.

To fix it, the two have launched Doomscrollr, a new social media platform with a single chronological feed and no shadowbanning. It claims to pull in everything you post across the internet to a single chronological feed. The product has been in beta and costs $99 to $1,999 per month for more robust features and customization. Natalie Jarvey wrote about the launch:

The idea for the company came from de la Fuente’s frustrations about how decentralized her presence on the internet had become. Outside of Substack, where she’s built an audience of more than 170,000 subscribers, she didn’t have a good picture of who her audience was or how to reach them. She wanted a curated feed of posts and links that would represent the full scope of her Zillion Trillion brand — and collect the email addresses of the people who were scrolling.

Doomscrollr essentially allows users to build a website with a feed of links and posts from across the internet. That means all their YouTube videos, Instagram photos, Substack posts and Shopify storefronts can sit in one feed that is organized chronologically or manually — no algorithm calculating what people see as they scroll.

As far as I can tell, Doomscrollr is the rare social tool aimed specifically at creators, creatives and entrepreneurs — what its founders refer to as “solopreneurs.” It’s been around for a little while as a paid product (pricing ranges from $99 per month to $1,999 per month depending on the level of customization) and has a number of high-profile users from creative industries including fashion designer Christopher John Rogers, creative director Alana Hadid and writer Arden Fanning Andrews, as well as brands like Nvidia and Dobel. Now the company is launching more widely with a free, public product.

Launching a new social platform in 2025 is a tough sell, but I can see the value in pulling in all of your content together into one hub. Other platforms have promised to do this in the past, and it seems to work well for link in bio type companies and personal websites.

The issue is that outside of some power users, I think the average consumer would probably prefer to consume content from their favorite creators natively within the different apps. But shadow banning is real and I do wish I had more autonomy over my feeds. I tried to sign up and test the platform out and so far it looks pretty bare bones (at least for the free version). Adam wrote a great piece for Rolling Stone earlier this year that explained why so many creators are desperate to own their own audience.

I think that, as the experience on social platforms degrades, more founders will build products that lie on top of the social web that try to mitigate the bad parts of these enshittifying platforms.
